title: A level Paper 3 mock — Set B: Microeconomics and macroeconomics
description: A synoptic Paper 3 drawing on all four themes. Section A is a data response on UK hospitality facing higher National Living Wage and employer National Insurance costs (costs, demand for labour, monopolistic competition and taxation); Section B is a data response on a trade dispute over electric cars in a fictional economy (tariffs, economies of scale, subsidies and supply-side policy). Each section has three data-response questions followed by a choice of 25-mark essay. Allow 2 hours: spend about 60 minutes on each section, including around 5 minutes reading the extracts and about 35 minutes on the essay. Show all workings in calculations, use the data throughout and finish each essay with a justified judgement.

questions.prompt: Using Table 1, calculate the percentage increase in the total annual cost to an employer of a full-time worker paid the National Living Wage between 2024-25 and 2025-26. Show your workings.
questions.context:
Rising costs in UK hospitality

Table 1: Annual cost to an employer of a full-time hospitality worker aged 21 or over paid the National Living Wage (NLW rates and employer National Insurance rules as they applied in each year; hours are illustrative)
Item | 2024-25 | 2025-26
National Living Wage (£ per hour) | 11.44 | 12.21
Hours worked per year | 1,560 | 1,560
Employer National Insurance contribution (NIC) rate (%) | 13.8 | 15.0
Annual earnings threshold above which employer NICs are paid (£) | 9,100 | 5,000
Note: ignore pension contributions and the Employment Allowance.

Table 2: Harbour Street Taverns, a fictional pub and restaurant group, 2023-2025 (illustrative data)
Year | Revenue (£m) | Staff costs (£m) | Energy and food costs (£m) | Operating profit (£m) | Number of sites | Employees
2023 | 210 | 66 | 71 | 18.0 | 140 | 5,600
2024 | 222 | 72 | 74 | 15.5 | 138 | 5,450
2025 | 230 | 80 | 76 | 9.8 | 129 | 5,050

Extract A: A tough year for pubs and restaurants
Hospitality is one of the UK's largest employers, with a high proportion of part-time, young and low-paid workers. The sector is made up of thousands of independent cafés, pubs and restaurants alongside a smaller number of chains such as Harbour Street Taverns. Consumers can choose between many outlets in most towns, and businesses compete through menus, atmosphere and location as much as through price. From April 2025 the National Living Wage rose by 6.7% and employers' National Insurance contributions increased. Industry surveys during 2025 reported that many operators had cut staff hours, frozen recruitment or raised menu prices, and a number of independent venues closed. Harbour Street Taverns has closed some of its least profitable sites and plans to introduce self-service ordering tablets in 60 of its pubs.

Extract B: Raising revenue
The government said the increase in employer NICs was needed to raise revenue for public services, including the NHS, without raising the main rates of income tax, employee National Insurance or VAT. At the same time it increased the Employment Allowance, which reduces the employer NICs bill of eligible employers, so that many of the smallest businesses pay less than before. Many economists expect that, over time, much of the cost of higher employer NICs will be passed on to workers through slower growth in pay than would otherwise have occurred, with some passed on to consumers through higher prices and some absorbed by firms through lower profits. The government's target is for the NLW to be at least two-thirds of median hourly earnings for workers aged 21 and over.

Extract C: Shortages, turnover and productivity
Despite job cuts in some areas, many hospitality employers in tourist areas still report difficulty recruiting chefs and front-of-house staff. Changes to immigration rules since 2021 have reduced the supply of EU workers to the sector, and staff turnover is high. Output per hour in hospitality is among the lowest of any UK sector. Supporters of higher minimum wages argue that they push firms to invest in training and technology, reduce costly staff turnover and raise the living standards of low-paid households. Critics argue that young and less-skilled workers will find it harder to get their first job, and that higher costs will be passed on as higher prices across the economy.
questions.mark_scheme:
Marking points:
1 mark for annual wage cost in both years: 2024-25: £11.44 x 1,560 = £17,846.40; 2025-26: £12.21 x 1,560 = £19,047.60.
1 mark for employer NICs in 2024-25: (£17,846.40 - £9,100) x 13.8% = £1,207.00 (accept £1,206.90 to £1,207.10).
1 mark for employer NICs in 2025-26: (£19,047.60 - £5,000) x 15% = £2,107.14.
1 mark for total annual cost in each year: 2024-25: £19,053.40; 2025-26: £21,154.74 (an increase of around £2,101).
1 mark for the percentage increase: (21,154.74 - 19,053.40) ÷ 19,053.40 x 100 = 11.0% (accept 11% or 11.03%).
Allow own-figure rule: if an earlier step contains an arithmetic error, award later marks where the method is correct. Credit (within the 5 marks, not in addition) a candidate who notes that the employer's cost rose by around 11%, well above the 6.7% rise in the NLW, because the NIC rate rose and the threshold fell.

questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: The demand for labour is a derived demand and is determined by the marginal revenue product of labour (MRP). A rise in the cost of employing labour (wages plus employer NICs) above the market-clearing wage reduces the quantity of labour demanded. The elasticity of demand for labour depends on the share of labour costs in total costs, the ease of substituting capital for labour, the price elasticity of demand for the final product and the time period.
Application: Employment cost per worker up around 11% (Table 1) compared with a 6.7% rise in the NLW; staff costs at Harbour Street rose from £66m to £80m and equal around 35% of revenue in 2025; employees fell from 5,450 to 5,050 (-7.3%) between 2024 and 2025 and sites from 138 to 129; self-service tablets in 60 pubs; many substitutes for eating out at any one venue.
Analysis: Diagram: labour market with demand (MRP) and supply of labour; a wage floor set above the equilibrium wage (W1 rising to W2, or a higher wage plus NICs) causes a contraction along the demand curve from Q1 to Qd, with an excess supply of labour (unemployment) of Qs - Qd. Chain 1: because labour is a large share of costs in a labour-intensive sector, a rise in employment costs raises average and marginal costs significantly, so firms cut hours and jobs; demand for labour is relatively elastic. Chain 2: firms substitute capital for labour (ordering tablets), and higher menu prices reduce the quantity of meals demanded, so the derived demand for labour falls further; in the long run, closures of sites (140 to 129) reduce employment in the industry.
Evaluation: The fall in employment at Harbour Street may also reflect higher energy and food costs and weaker consumer spending, so not all of it is caused by labour costs. If employers have monopsony power, a higher minimum wage can raise employment, though this is less likely in a sector with many employers. Labour shortages and high turnover (Extract C) suggest the equilibrium wage in some areas may be above the NLW, so the effect is smaller there. Over time, much of the NIC cost may be passed on in slower pay growth, limiting job losses. The Employment Allowance reduces the effect on the smallest employers.
Mark split: Knowledge, Application and Analysis up to 6 marks; Evaluation up to 2 marks.
Levels (Knowledge, Application, Analysis):
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Isolated knowledge with little or no use of the data or context; analysis is absent or a list of assertions; any diagram is inaccurate or not used.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with some reference to the data; one or two chains of reasoning that are partly developed; diagram broadly accurate but not fully integrated.
Level 3 (5-6 marks): Precise knowledge applied consistently to the context and figures; two clear, logical and well-linked chains of reasoning; accurate diagram fully explained and integrated where required.
Levels (Evaluation):
Level 1 (1 mark): A generic or asserted evaluative comment.
Level 2 (2 marks): A developed, supported evaluative point that is applied to the context (for example magnitude, time period or what the outcome depends on).
A* answer: Draws an accurate labour market diagram with a wage floor above equilibrium, uses the 11% rise in employment costs and the fall in Harbour Street's workforce, explains why demand for labour is relatively elastic in hospitality (labour share, substitution, elastic product demand), and evaluates using other cost pressures, monopsony, labour shortages and pass-through to pay.

questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Monopolistic competition: many firms, low barriers to entry and exit, differentiated products, and a downward-sloping but relatively elastic demand curve. Firms profit maximise where MC = MR. In the short run firms may make supernormal profit or losses; in the long run entry and exit ensure normal profit, with AR tangent to AC.
Application: Many independents and some chains; competition through menus, atmosphere and location (Extract A). Harbour Street's operating profit fell from £18.0m to £9.8m and its margin from around 8.6% of revenue (2023) to around 4.3% (2025); revenue rose from £210m to £230m (+9.5%) while staff costs rose by around 21%; sites fell from 140 to 129; independent venues closed.
Analysis: Short run: higher wage, NIC, energy and food costs shift MC and AC upwards; the profit-maximising output falls and price rises, but because each firm faces relatively elastic demand (close substitutes), it cannot pass on all of the increase without losing customers, so profit margins are squeezed, as Harbour Street's data show; firms with weak positions make losses. Because all firms in the industry face the same cost increase, each can raise prices with less risk of losing customers to rivals, so industry prices rise more than a single firm acting alone could achieve. Long run: firms making losses leave the market (closures of sites and independents), so demand shifts to the remaining firms; their demand curves shift right until AR is again tangent to AC and the remaining firms earn normal profit at a higher price and lower industry output. Consumers face higher prices and less choice. Firms may also respond by cutting costs (tablets, fewer staff), raising productivity.
Evaluation: Ability to pass on costs depends on product differentiation and brand loyalty: chains with strong brands or prime locations may protect margins better than independents. Consumer incomes matter: hospitality is income elastic, so if real incomes are rising demand may hold up, but in a downturn price rises cut sales sharply. Chains benefit from economies of scale in purchasing and technology; small firms gain from the Employment Allowance, so the impact differs by size. The model's assumption of free entry may not hold: rising costs and lost confidence may deter entry, and some firms may be in local oligopolies or have objectives other than profit maximisation (lifestyle businesses may satisfice). Revenue growth of 9.5% suggests some cost pass-through, but not enough to protect profit. Judgement required on how far prices rise and whether long-run profits are restored.
Mark split: Knowledge, Application and Analysis up to 8 marks; Evaluation up to 4 marks.
Levels (Knowledge, Application, Analysis):
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Isolated or partially accurate knowledge; little or no application to the context or data; analysis is absent or consists of unconnected assertions.
Level 2 (3-5 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with some use of the data; relevant chains of reasoning that may be incomplete or one-sided; diagrams, if used, may contain minor errors.
Level 3 (6-8 marks): Precise, relevant knowledge applied consistently to the context and data; clear, logical and well-linked chains of reasoning covering more than one side of the issue, supported by accurate diagrams or calculations where relevant.
Levels (Evaluation):
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Evaluation is generic or asserted, with little reference to the context; any judgement is unsupported.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Balanced evaluation supported by the data and context, weighing the significance of the arguments and reaching a justified judgement.
A* answer: Identifies the market as monopolistically competitive with evidence, uses Harbour Street's falling margin (8.6% to 4.3%) and site closures, analyses short-run losses and long-run exit restoring normal profit with accurate diagrams, recognises that industry-wide cost shocks are easier to pass on, and evaluates using differentiation, income elasticity, firm size and the realism of free entry.

questions.mark_scheme:
This mark scheme covers both options. Mark the option the candidate has chosen using the indicative content for that option and the shared level descriptors.

OPTION (a): Employer National Insurance as a revenue raiser
Knowledge: Direct and indirect taxes; tax incidence (formal versus effective); progressive, proportional and regressive taxes; the Laffer curve; economic effects of taxation on incentives, labour demand, real output and employment, income distribution and the government budget; fiscal policy and public sector finances.
Application: Employer cost per NLW worker up around 11%, of which NICs rose from around £1,207 to £2,107 (Table 1); the government chose not to raise income tax, employee NICs or VAT (Extract B); expected pass-through to workers, consumers and profits; Employment Allowance protects small firms; hospitality job losses and site closures (Table 2); the UK's large current budget pressures from health and debt interest.
Analysis: Employer NICs have a broad base (all employees above the threshold), so a small rate change raises a large amount of revenue at low administrative cost, which can fund public services or reduce the deficit. Because the tax is levied on employers, its visible burden on households is small, which may make it politically easier than raising income tax. However, the effective incidence falls largely on workers through lower pay growth, so it acts like a tax on labour income; lowering the threshold to £5,000 makes it bite harder on part-time and low-paid workers, making it less progressive. It raises the cost of employing labour, reducing demand for labour, particularly in labour-intensive sectors such as hospitality and social care, and encourages substitution of capital for labour; this can raise unemployment and reduce income tax receipts, partly offsetting the revenue gain. Higher costs may be passed on in prices, adding to cost-push inflation. Lower profits reduce retained earnings and investment, reducing LRAS. Spending the revenue on the NHS may raise productivity and labour supply (fewer people out of work through ill health), supporting long-run growth.
Evaluation: The net revenue depends on behavioural responses: if employment and pay fall, income tax and NIC receipts fall, so net yield is below the static estimate (Laffer-style effects, though the UK is unlikely to be beyond the revenue-maximising rate). Effects differ by sector and firm size; the Employment Allowance concentrates the burden on larger employers. Alternatives such as raising income tax, property taxes or closing reliefs may be fairer or less damaging to employment. The impact depends on the state of the economy: in a weak labour market more of the cost falls on jobs. Judgement required on effectiveness, weighing large and reliable revenue against its effects on employment, pay and growth.

OPTION (b): Macroeconomic effects of large real increases in the National Living Wage
Knowledge: Minimum wage as a wage floor; macroeconomic objectives (growth, low unemployment, low inflation, equity, balance of payments); AD and AS; cost-push inflation; the Phillips curve; relative and absolute poverty; productivity and international competitiveness; unit labour costs.
Application: NLW up 6.7% in 2025 to £12.21; target of at least two-thirds of median hourly earnings (Extract B); hospitality job and hours cuts, site closures; labour shortages, high turnover and low productivity in hospitality (Extract C); low-paid, young and part-time workers.
Analysis: Higher pay for low-paid workers raises their disposable income; because low-income households have a high marginal propensity to consume, consumption and AD rise, with multiplier effects on output and employment. It reduces relative poverty and income inequality and reduces spending on in-work benefits, improving public finances. On the supply side, higher wages can raise productivity through efficiency wage effects, lower turnover and greater incentives to invest in training and capital, shifting LRAS right. Against: higher unit labour costs shift SRAS left, causing cost-push inflation and lower output; if workers further up the pay scale seek to restore differentials, a wage-price spiral may follow. Real increases that outstrip productivity raise unemployment among the young and low-skilled, possibly raising structural unemployment. UK firms facing higher unit labour costs may lose international competitiveness, worsening the trade balance in traded sectors. Higher inflation may require tighter monetary policy.
Evaluation: The overall effect depends on the size of the increase relative to median earnings and productivity growth; evidence from the UK since 1999 suggests modest minimum wage increases had small effects on employment, but very large increases are less tested. Many low-paid jobs are in non-traded services (hospitality, care), so the effect on international competitiveness may be small. Effects vary by region: in areas with lower median pay the NLW bites harder. Firms may respond with fewer hours, lower non-wage benefits or more automation rather than job cuts. Monopsony employers may increase employment. Benefit withdrawal (tapers in Universal Credit) means low-paid households keep only part of a pay rise, limiting the effect on poverty. Judgement required on whether the equity and productivity gains outweigh risks to employment and inflation.

Mark split: Knowledge, Application and Analysis up to 16 marks; Evaluation up to 9 marks. The same levels apply to option (a) and option (b).
Levels (Knowledge, Application, Analysis):
Level 1 (1-4 marks): Some relevant knowledge, often definitions only; little application to the extracts or the wider economy; analysis is descriptive or confused.
Level 2 (5-8 marks): Accurate knowledge with some relevant application to the extracts; one or two chains of reasoning developed but partial or one-sided; diagrams may be present but are not fully explained.
Level 3 (9-12 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the extracts and to real-world examples; several developed chains of reasoning across micro and macro issues, with appropriate diagrams; some synoptic links between themes.
Level 4 (13-16 marks): Precise, wide-ranging knowledge applied throughout to the data and well-chosen examples; fully developed, logical chains of reasoning with accurate, integrated diagrams; clear synoptic links between microeconomic and macroeconomic effects.
Levels (Evaluation):
Level 1 (1-3 marks): Evaluation is generic or asserted; little reference to the evidence; any conclusion is unsupported.
Level 2 (4-6 marks): Evaluation is present across the answer and considers alternative outcomes, uses some evidence from the extracts, but is not consistently supported or prioritised.
Level 3 (7-9 marks): Sustained evaluation that weighs arguments using the data, considers magnitude, time period, stakeholders and assumptions, prioritises the most significant factors and reaches a fully justified overall judgement.
A* answer: For (a), uses Table 1 to show how the NIC change raised employer costs, distinguishes formal from effective incidence, analyses revenue, labour demand, inflation and investment effects, compares employer NICs with alternative taxes and reaches a justified judgement on effectiveness. For (b), analyses AD (high MPC of the low paid), SRAS and LRAS effects with diagrams, links to unemployment, inflation, inequality and competitiveness, and evaluates using the size of increases relative to productivity, sector and regional differences, monopsony and benefit tapers.

questions.prompt: Using Table 1 and Extract A, calculate (i) the price of an average Asterland EV in Veldonia after the 25% tariff, (ii) the expected tariff revenue in 2026, and (iii) the expected percentage fall in imports from Asterland between 2025 and 2026. Explain why Asterland EVs are still likely to sell in large numbers.
questions.context:
Electric cars and a trade dispute (illustrative data)

Veldonia is a fictional high-income economy with a large car industry and a floating currency, the Veldonian crown (VC). Asterland is a fictional upper-middle-income economy that has become the world's largest producer of electric vehicles (EVs) and EV batteries.

Table 1: Veldonia's market for new electric cars, 2022-2025 (illustrative data)
Year | New EV sales in Veldonia (thousands) | Of which imported from Asterland (thousands) | Average price of an Asterland EV in Veldonia before any tariff (VC) | Average price of a Veldonian-made EV (VC)
2022 | 300 | 30 | 24,000 | 38,000
2023 | 420 | 80 | 22,500 | 37,000
2024 | 560 | 150 | 21,000 | 36,500
2025 | 650 | 200 | 20,000 | 36,000

Table 2: Estimated average cost of producing an EV battery pack at different annual plant outputs (illustrative data)
Annual output of plant (thousand packs) | 50 | 200 | 500 | 1,000
Average cost per pack (VC) | 14,000 | 9,500 | 7,000 | 6,200

Extract A: A new tariff
In January 2026 Veldonia's government imposed a 25% tariff on EVs imported from Asterland. It argues that Asterland's producers benefit from state support, including cheap land, cheap electricity and loans from state-owned banks, which allows them to sell below the cost faced by unsubsidised producers. Forecasters expect imports from Asterland to fall to around 120,000 cars in 2026, assuming the pre-tariff price stays at VC20,000. Some Asterland producers plan to build assembly plants inside Veldonia to avoid the tariff. Asterland's government has threatened to impose retaliatory tariffs on Veldonian wine, aircraft parts and luxury cars.

Extract B: Scale and the climate
Battery production has very high fixed costs: a large plant can cost several billion crowns to build, and the battery is the most expensive part of an EV. Veldonia's largest battery plant produces around 120,000 packs a year, while Asterland's leading producers each make more than one million. Veldonia has a target that all new cars sold from 2035 must be zero-emission. Petrol and diesel cars create negative externalities through carbon emissions and local air pollution. Veldonia currently offers no subsidy for buying an EV. Motoring groups argue that a grant of VC4,000 per new EV would speed up switching, but the finance ministry warns that it would cost around VC2.6 billion a year at 2025 sales levels, and that much of it would go to higher-income households who would have bought an EV anyway.

Extract C: Jobs, prices and strategy
Around 400,000 people work in Veldonia's car industry, mostly in two northern regions where unemployment is above the national average. Domestic carmakers say they need time to reach the scale of their Asterland rivals. Consumer groups argue that the tariff will raise prices for households and slow the switch to EVs, at a time when Veldonia's inflation rate is 3.4%, above the central bank's 2% target. Some economists argue that the government should instead adopt an industrial strategy: subsidising battery 'gigafactories', funding training in battery engineering, investing in public charging points and speeding up planning decisions, while keeping its markets open to imports. Others warn that governments are poor at 'picking winners' and that subsidy races between countries waste taxpayers' money.

Marking points:

2 marks for (ii): VC5,000 x 120,000 = VC600 million (VC0.6 billion). Award 1 mark for the correct method with an arithmetic error, or for using 200,000 cars (VC1 billion) with the method shown.

questions.prompt: With reference to Table 2 and Extract B, examine, using a diagram, why producers in Asterland may be able to sell EVs at lower prices than Veldonian producers.
questions.context:
Electric cars and a trade dispute (illustrative data)

Veldonia is a fictional high-income economy with a large car industry and a floating currency, the Veldonian crown (VC). Asterland is a fictional upper-middle-income economy that has become the world's largest producer of electric vehicles (EVs) and EV batteries.

Table 1: Veldonia's market for new electric cars, 2022-2025 (illustrative data)
Year | New EV sales in Veldonia (thousands) | Of which imported from Asterland (thousands) | Average price of an Asterland EV in Veldonia before any tariff (VC) | Average price of a Veldonian-made EV (VC)
2022 | 300 | 30 | 24,000 | 38,000
2023 | 420 | 80 | 22,500 | 37,000
2024 | 560 | 150 | 21,000 | 36,500
2025 | 650 | 200 | 20,000 | 36,000

Table 2: Estimated average cost of producing an EV battery pack at different annual plant outputs (illustrative data)
Annual output of plant (thousand packs) | 50 | 200 | 500 | 1,000
Average cost per pack (VC) | 14,000 | 9,500 | 7,000 | 6,200

Extract A: A new tariff
In January 2026 Veldonia's government imposed a 25% tariff on EVs imported from Asterland. It argues that Asterland's producers benefit from state support, including cheap land, cheap electricity and loans from state-owned banks, which allows them to sell below the cost faced by unsubsidised producers. Forecasters expect imports from Asterland to fall to around 120,000 cars in 2026, assuming the pre-tariff price stays at VC20,000. Some Asterland producers plan to build assembly plants inside Veldonia to avoid the tariff. Asterland's government has threatened to impose retaliatory tariffs on Veldonian wine, aircraft parts and luxury cars.

Extract B: Scale and the climate
Battery production has very high fixed costs: a large plant can cost several billion crowns to build, and the battery is the most expensive part of an EV. Veldonia's largest battery plant produces around 120,000 packs a year, while Asterland's leading producers each make more than one million. Veldonia has a target that all new cars sold from 2035 must be zero-emission. Petrol and diesel cars create negative externalities through carbon emissions and local air pollution. Veldonia currently offers no subsidy for buying an EV. Motoring groups argue that a grant of VC4,000 per new EV would speed up switching, but the finance ministry warns that it would cost around VC2.6 billion a year at 2025 sales levels, and that much of it would go to higher-income households who would have bought an EV anyway.

Extract C: Jobs, prices and strategy
Around 400,000 people work in Veldonia's car industry, mostly in two northern regions where unemployment is above the national average. Domestic carmakers say they need time to reach the scale of their Asterland rivals. Consumer groups argue that the tariff will raise prices for households and slow the switch to EVs, at a time when Veldonia's inflation rate is 3.4%, above the central bank's 2% target. Some economists argue that the government should instead adopt an industrial strategy: subsidising battery 'gigafactories', funding training in battery engineering, investing in public charging points and speeding up planning decisions, while keeping its markets open to imports. Others warn that governments are poor at 'picking winners' and that subsidy races between countries waste taxpayers' money.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Internal economies of scale: falling long-run average cost as the scale of output increases, for example technical economies (spreading high fixed costs, larger and more efficient machinery), purchasing economies (bulk buying of lithium and other materials) and financial economies. Minimum efficient scale (MES). External economies of scale from the growth of an industry in one location (suppliers, skilled labour, research).
Application: Table 2: average cost per pack falls from VC14,000 at 50,000 packs to VC6,200 at one million, a fall of around 56%; Veldonia's largest plant makes around 120,000 packs (average cost somewhere between VC9,500 and VC14,000), while Asterland's leaders make over one million (around VC6,200), so the cost gap per pack is at least VC3,300; the battery is the most expensive part of an EV; Asterland EVs sold at VC20,000 against VC36,000 in 2025; state support in Asterland (Extract A).
Analysis: Diagram: a downward-sloping LRAC curve with Veldonian producers at a low output (Q1) and high average cost (AC1), and Asterland producers at a much larger output (Q2) near the MES with lower average cost (AC2). Chain 1: battery plants have very high fixed costs; spreading them over a million packs instead of 120,000 sharply lowers average fixed cost, so Asterland producers have lower unit costs and can set lower prices while still covering costs. Chain 2: Asterland's large industry creates external economies of scale (clusters of component suppliers, specialised labour, learning by doing), shifting its whole LRAC curve down relative to Veldonia's. Lower costs allow lower prices, which raise sales and allow further scale economies in a self-reinforcing cycle.
Evaluation: Lower prices may also reflect state subsidies, cheaper labour and energy, or an undervalued currency, not only economies of scale, so the extent of the cost advantage is uncertain. Table 2 shows diminishing gains from scale beyond 500,000 packs (VC7,000 to VC6,200), so once Veldonian producers reach a moderate scale the gap narrows. Very large firms may face diseconomies of scale. Asterland producers' prices also include transport costs and, from 2026, the tariff.
Mark split: Knowledge, Application and Analysis up to 6 marks; Evaluation up to 2 marks.
Levels (Knowledge, Application, Analysis):
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Isolated knowledge with little or no use of the data or context; analysis is absent or a list of assertions; any diagram is inaccurate or not used.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with some reference to the data; one or two chains of reasoning that are partly developed; diagram broadly accurate but not fully integrated.
Level 3 (5-6 marks): Precise knowledge applied consistently to the context and figures; two clear, logical and well-linked chains of reasoning; accurate diagram fully explained and integrated where required.
Levels (Evaluation):
Level 1 (1 mark): A generic or asserted evaluative comment.
Level 2 (2 marks): A developed, supported evaluative point that is applied to the context (for example magnitude, time period or what the outcome depends on).
A* answer: Uses Table 2 to quantify the cost gap at the two plant sizes, draws an accurate LRAC diagram showing the two firms' positions relative to MES, develops technical and external economies of scale, and evaluates by separating scale effects from state subsidies and noting diminishing returns to scale beyond 500,000 packs.

questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Negative externalities from petrol and diesel cars (MSC > MPC) and possible positive externalities from EV adoption (lower emissions, network effects from charging infrastructure, learning). A subsidy shifts supply to the right, lowering price and increasing quantity; cost of the subsidy to the government; incidence of a subsidy between consumers and producers; government failure.
Application: Subsidy of VC4,000 compared with average EV prices of VC20,000-36,000; estimated cost VC2.6 billion a year at 2025 sales (650,000 x VC4,000) (Extract B); 2035 zero-emission target; much would go to higher-income households; inflation of 3.4% (Extract C); 200,000 of the 650,000 EVs in 2025 were imported from Asterland.
Analysis: For: the subsidy lowers the effective price of EVs relative to petrol cars, encouraging consumers to switch; diagram showing supply shifting from S to S - subsidy, with quantity rising towards the social optimum where the marginal social benefit of EVs (including avoided emissions) equals cost. Faster switching reduces carbon and air pollution, helps meet the 2035 target and supports a larger market, which helps domestic producers reach economies of scale. For consumers, the subsidy helps overcome high upfront cost and present bias (behavioural economics), and increased EV numbers justify more charging points. Against: deadweight: many buyers would have bought EVs anyway, so the cost per additional EV is high; the benefits go disproportionately to higher-income households, so the policy is regressive. With inelastic supply, much of the subsidy may be captured by producers through higher prices. A large share of the subsidy would go to buyers of imported Asterland cars, adding to import demand. The VC2.6 billion cost has an opportunity cost (charging points, public transport) and, if borrowed, adds to the deficit and to AD at a time of above-target inflation.
Evaluation: The case depends on the price elasticity of demand for EVs: if demand is elastic the subsidy has a large effect on take-up. Design features can improve value for money: means-testing, a price cap on eligible cars, or a tapering scheme as EV prices fall. Alternatives such as a carbon tax on fuel, regulation (the 2035 target and fleet emissions standards), or investment in charging infrastructure may be cheaper per tonne of carbon saved. Government failure risks: information gaps about the social benefit and difficulty removing the subsidy later. The tariff (raising prices) and the subsidy (lowering them) work in opposite directions, so policy coherence is a concern. Judgement required: for example, a targeted, time-limited subsidy may be justified, but a universal VC4,000 grant is costly and poorly targeted.
Mark split: Knowledge, Application and Analysis up to 8 marks; Evaluation up to 4 marks.
Levels (Knowledge, Application, Analysis):
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Isolated or partially accurate knowledge; little or no application to the context or data; analysis is absent or consists of unconnected assertions.
Level 2 (3-5 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with some use of the data; relevant chains of reasoning that may be incomplete or one-sided; diagrams, if used, may contain minor errors.
Level 3 (6-8 marks): Precise, relevant knowledge applied consistently to the context and data; clear, logical and well-linked chains of reasoning covering more than one side of the issue, supported by accurate diagrams or calculations where relevant.
Levels (Evaluation):
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Evaluation is generic or asserted, with little reference to the context; any judgement is unsupported.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Balanced evaluation supported by the data and context, weighing the significance of the arguments and reaching a justified judgement.
A* answer: Uses the VC2.6 billion cost and price data, draws an accurate subsidy diagram linked to externalities, weighs faster switching and scale effects against deadweight cost, regressive incidence, import leakage and inflation, compares alternatives such as carbon pricing and charging infrastructure, and reaches a justified judgement on design.

(a) Using the information provided and your own knowledge, evaluate the likely effects of the 25% tariff on EVs imported from Asterland on Veldonia's economy.

(b) Using the information provided and your own knowledge, evaluate whether supply-side policies, such as the industrial strategy described in Extract C, are likely to be more effective than tariffs in supporting Veldonia's car industry and its wider economy.

questions.mark_scheme:
This mark scheme covers both options. Mark the option the candidate has chosen using the indicative content for that option and the shared level descriptors.

OPTION (a): Effects of the 25% tariff
Knowledge: Tariffs as a restriction on free trade; tariff diagram showing world price, domestic supply and demand, imports, tariff revenue, changes in consumer and producer surplus and deadweight welfare losses; infant industry and anti-dumping arguments; retaliation and trade wars; WTO rules; effects on AD, inflation and the current account.
Application: Tariff raises the Asterland price from VC20,000 to VC25,000; imports expected to fall 40% to 120,000; tariff revenue around VC600 million; Asterland EVs still around 31% cheaper than Veldonian EVs; 400,000 car workers in regions with above-average unemployment; inflation 3.4% above the 2% target; threatened retaliation against wine, aircraft parts and luxury cars; Asterland producers may build plants in Veldonia; 2035 zero-emission target.
Analysis: Tariff diagram: price rises from world price Pw to Pw + t; domestic output rises, imports fall, consumer surplus falls, producer surplus and government revenue rise, and there are two deadweight losses (production and consumption distortions). Micro: domestic producers gain sales and time to reach economies of scale (infant industry argument), protecting jobs in the northern regions; but higher prices reduce consumer surplus and slow EV adoption, increasing negative externalities from petrol cars. Reduced competitive pressure may cause X-inefficiency in domestic firms. Macro: lower imports and more domestic production raise net exports and AD, with regional multiplier effects; the current account may improve. However, higher EV prices add to cost-push inflation when inflation is already above target, possibly prompting higher interest rates. Retaliation reduces exports of wine, aircraft parts and luxury cars, reducing AD and harming jobs in those sectors. If Asterland firms build plants in Veldonia (tariff-jumping FDI), this creates jobs, transfers technology and raises LRAS.
Evaluation: Effects depend on PED for imported EVs and the price gap: with a VC11,000 gap many buyers will still choose imports, so protection is limited while consumers pay more. If Asterland is genuinely subsidising exports, the tariff may correct an unfair advantage and be WTO-compatible as a countervailing duty. Whether domestic firms use the protection to invest and become competitive, or remain inefficient, is uncertain; infant industry protection is hard to remove. The scale of retaliation matters: if it is limited to small sectors, the net effect on AD may be small. Short run versus long run: jobs may be protected now, but the slower EV transition and higher prices may harm living standards and climate targets. Justified judgement required.

OPTION (b): Supply-side industrial strategy versus tariffs
Knowledge: Supply-side policies: interventionist (subsidies for investment, training, infrastructure, industrial strategy) and market-based (deregulation, faster planning); effects on LRAS, productivity and international competitiveness; tariffs and protectionism; government failure, including 'picking winners' and regulatory capture; economies of scale; comparative advantage; opportunity cost.
Application: Battery cost falls from VC14,000 to VC6,200 per pack with scale (Table 2); Veldonia's largest plant produces 120,000 packs against over one million in Asterland; gigafactory subsidies, training in battery engineering, charging points, faster planning (Extract C); 400,000 car workers; inflation of 3.4%; warnings about subsidy races.
Analysis: Supply-side support addresses the cause of the competitiveness gap: subsidising gigafactories helps Veldonian producers reach minimum efficient scale, lowering average cost towards Asterland's levels; training raises labour productivity and reduces skills shortages; charging infrastructure increases demand for all EVs and corrects a coordination failure. These shift LRAS to the right, raising potential growth without raising prices, and so avoid the cost-push inflation and consumer welfare losses caused by tariffs. Keeping markets open maintains competitive pressure and dynamic efficiency, allows consumers to benefit from cheap imports (helping the 2035 target), and avoids retaliation against exporters. Tariffs, by contrast, act quickly, raise revenue and give immediate protection to jobs, and may be justified as a response to unfair subsidies abroad.
Evaluation: Supply-side policies have long time lags (years to build plants and train workers), while jobs in car regions are at risk now; tariffs may buy time for the supply-side measures to work, so the two may be complements rather than substitutes. Industrial strategy has a large fiscal cost and opportunity cost, and governments lack information about which technologies and firms will succeed (government failure); subsidy races between countries may transfer taxpayers' money to multinational firms without creating lasting advantage. If Asterland's cost advantage reflects comparative advantage and large external economies of scale, Veldonia may be better off specialising in other parts of the supply chain (design, software, premium models). Success depends on scale: Table 2 suggests plants need around 500,000 packs to get close to the lowest costs, which may require a large share of Veldonia's market. Justified judgement required.

Mark split: Knowledge, Application and Analysis up to 16 marks; Evaluation up to 9 marks. The same levels apply to option (a) and option (b).
Levels (Knowledge, Application, Analysis):
Level 1 (1-4 marks): Some relevant knowledge, often definitions only; little application to the extracts or the wider economy; analysis is descriptive or confused.
Level 2 (5-8 marks): Accurate knowledge with some relevant application to the extracts; one or two chains of reasoning developed but partial or one-sided; diagrams may be present but are not fully explained.
Level 3 (9-12 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the extracts and to real-world examples; several developed chains of reasoning across micro and macro issues, with appropriate diagrams; some synoptic links between themes.
Level 4 (13-16 marks): Precise, wide-ranging knowledge applied throughout to the data and well-chosen examples; fully developed, logical chains of reasoning with accurate, integrated diagrams; clear synoptic links between microeconomic and macroeconomic effects.
Levels (Evaluation):
Level 1 (1-3 marks): Evaluation is generic or asserted; little reference to the evidence; any conclusion is unsupported.
Level 2 (4-6 marks): Evaluation is present across the answer and considers alternative outcomes, uses some evidence from the extracts, but is not consistently supported or prioritised.
Level 3 (7-9 marks): Sustained evaluation that weighs arguments using the data, considers magnitude, time period, stakeholders and assumptions, prioritises the most significant factors and reaches a fully justified overall judgement.
A* answer: For (a), draws and fully explains a tariff diagram using the VC5,000 tariff and 40% fall in imports, traces micro effects on consumers, producers and externalities and macro effects on AD, inflation, the current account and retaliation, and judges the overall effect over the short and long run. For (b), analyses how gigafactory subsidies, training and infrastructure shift LRAS and close the cost gap shown in Table 2, compares this with the immediate but distorting effects of tariffs, weighs time lags, fiscal cost and government failure, and reaches a justified judgement, for example that the policies are most effective in combination.
